title: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism
description: How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of womenFigure caption, Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equalityByTi
body: How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of womenFigure caption, Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equalityByTiffany WertheimerUpdated 12:26 BSTGloria Steinem was a powerful icon of America's feminist movement and her career spanned numerous roles that changed the lives of generations of women.With her iconic aviator sunglasses and long, blonde-streaked hair - which she considered rebellious in the 1970s - Steinem was an internationally recognised activist in the fight for women's equality.She spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage, and equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.Her activism was not without a backlash - from both men and women - and harassment that could be as vulgar as it was intimidating.The early yearsBorn on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, Gloria Steinem did not have an easy childhood.Her father Leo Steinem was a travelling salesman and, together with her mother Ruth and older sister Susanne, they lived in a caravan, crisscrossing the country.Leo abandoned the family and moved to California when Steinem was 10 years old, leaving her to care for Ruth who had long suffered with mental illness and had terrifying hallucinations. As a result, Steinem did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gloria Steinem at the 1972 Democratic ConventionShe would later remark that she had never wanted children because she had already had one - her mother.In the late 1950s she went to India on a research scholarship, and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.Steinem left India and moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. It was a time when male-dominated newsrooms made it difficult for women to get hard-hitting stories.Breakthrough articleHer big break came in 1963, when Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny cocktail waitress and wrote A Bunny's Tale, an exposé for Show magazine detailing the seedy and sexist reality of Hugh Hefner's empire.As soon as she arrived for the interview, a security guard called out, "Here bunny, bunny, bunny."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steinem's undercover work as a Playboy Bunny revealed a world of misogyny and exploitationUsing the fake name Marie, she lied about her age - telling Playboy she was 24 years old when she was actually four years older.Steinem lifted the lid on the underpaid life of a Bunny, and the physical pain of wearing the high-heels and tight corsets for hours.Despite the fame - and infamy - that followed, she still found herself struggling to be taken seriously by editors. Though the Playboy exposé helped land her assignments for the New York Times and New York Magazine, often they were about ladies' stockings and the latest hairstyles."To this day when people don't like me they introduce me as a former Bunny, as a put-down," she told the New York Times in 2016. "On the other hand, I did improve the working conditions for those women."All-female journalismUndaunted, by 1968 Steinem was a columnist for New York Magazine, focusing on progressive social issues and women's rights.Her article, After Black Power, Women's Liberation, external brought her national fame, making her the face of the US feminist movement in the 1970s."I was the only woman, and after I wrote an abortion article, my [male] friends there said to me: 'Don't get involved with these crazy women. You've worked hard to be taken seriously,'" she told Rachel Cooke for The Guardian in 2011.So she took matters into her own hands.In 1972, she launched Ms. magazine with a group of feminist activists. It was the first all-female founded and operated periodical, designed to be an alternative to other women's magazines that typically focused on housekeeping and fashion.Image source, EPAImage caption, Ms. magazine broke new ground, selling out within its first week of publicationCritics - mainly men - were quick to write it off. News presenter Harry Reasoner said he gave it six months "before they run out of things to say".The first issue sold out within a week and generated 26,000 subscribers. The magazine is still going today.In 1978, Steinem wrote one of Ms. magazine's most infamous and widely read essays - If Men Could Menstruate. Her satirical reflection on how different power, political and economic structures might be if men had menstrual cycles is still referred to in discussions about gender roles.By the end of her career, Steinem had become a prolific and award-winning writer, penning numerous books including her own memoirs, a biography on Marilyn Monroe and a collection of her own famous quotes in the wryly titled, ‪The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off.Abortion rights campaignerThough still considered one of the world's best-known feminist activists, Steinem came to advocacy rather late in life - in her thirties.At an abortion awareness rally in 1969 where women were sharing their experiences of having abortions, Steinem was encouraged to share her own story about terminating a pregnancy. It had taken place years earlier in London when she was 22 years old, just before going to India.Abortion was illegal in the UK at the time, unless the woman's mental or physical health was in danger. The doctor took a great risk for Steinem, telling her: "You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."Nearly 60 years later, Steinem broke one of those promises, when she dedicated her memoir, My Life On The Road, to Dr John Sharpe.She described that abortion speak-out event as a "light bulb moment" - when she realised the US needed a bigger women's rights movement.Almost overnight, Steinem became a crusader for abortion rights, calling it "reproductive freedom". The phrase she coined is credited with making the subject more approachable for political discussion and continues to be used in abortion debates.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Joining Steinem at the 1989 March for Women’s Lives were Susan Sarandon, Gloria Allred, Jesse Jackson and Jane FondaSteinem organised marches and quickly became a draw at demonstrations, although she admitted later that she found talking to the huge crowds "utterly terrifying".After Congress failed to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1970 - legislation granting women equal rights to men - Steinem co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus with fellow feminist leaders and more than 300 women across the US. The group worked to include women in all aspects of political and public life.The same year, she testified at Senate hearings for the ERA, telling the predominantly male audience: "I have been refused service in public restaurants, ordered out of public gathering places and turned away from apartment rentals all for the clearly stated, sole reason that I am a woman."Second-wave feminism continued to gain momentum and Steinem was one of its most famous figureheads.She was also supportive of same-sex marriage, but was criticised for an essay she wrote in 1977 on transgender people. She clarified her position in 2013, saying the words in her "old essay" had been taken "out of time and context"."I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned," she wrote in an opinion piece, external.Steinem was also criticised for a 1998 essay in the New York Times, where she showed support for then-President Bill Clinton after news broke of his scandalous affair with intern Monica Lewinsky - who was 22 years old at the time."The truth is that even if the allegations are true, the president is not guilty of sexual harassment," Steinem wrote. "He is accused of having made a gross, dumb and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life."In 2017, she said she "wouldn't write the same thing now".Too glamorous?Critics came from the left as well as right, targeting Steinem for everything from her looks to her motives. Some claimed she was too glamorous to be a true feminist, while others said she was successful only because of her appearance.Betty Friedan, author of The Feminine Mystique, the book credited with launching second-wave feminism, was annoyed that Steinem became the face of the movement, accusing her of "ripping off the movement for private profit" when she launched Ms.The media were trying "to make her a celebrity," fumed Friedan, "but no one should mistake her for a leader."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steinem's sudden rise to become the face of second-wave feminism caught the ire of some activistsUS President Richard Nixon was recorded during a secret conversation furiously ranting about Steinem, to which she responded: "There is some opinion that Richard Nixon is the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon".Al Goldstein, the notorious pornographer and publisher of Screw magazine, launched a campaign of attacks that included publishing her phone number next to fake advertisements for oral sex.He also printed a graphic centrefold image of a Steinem look-alike, and hung it open on display at the newsstand outside Ms. magazine's office building. She had to look at it every day.As she got older, harassment to this degree became less common. However, given she was a recognisable figure in New York City, it was not uncommon for Steinem to be stopped on the street by strangers wanting to debate - sometimes with an edge of hostility.But she welcomed the continued debate. In 2020, she was among a cross-section of public figures who signed an open letter denouncing cancel culture, saying it weakens open debate by shutting people down."If you care about having the conversation, surely you want to try in a humane way to convince the other person, not do away with them," she told the New York Times.'I can't mate in captivity'Gloria Steinem once quipped: "I can't mate in captivity" - a reference to her disinterest in marriage. But she publicly enjoyed a healthy dating life with a number of rich and famous bachelors, giving critics more ammunition to use against her.They included Frank Thomas who was head of the Ford Foundation; film director Mike Nichols and Olympic decathlete Rafer Johnson (who helped tackle the man who assassinated Robert F Kennedy in 1968)."I was the one always accused of using men, of being too sexual. Someone once sent me a cartoon of a tombstone that said 'at last she sleeps alone'," she wrote.But in 2000, aged 66, she wed David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist, and father of actor Christian Bale.At the time, the union drew gasps of surprise and even disappointment from some feminists, who had spent years following Steinem's heated debates surrounding marriage laws.But she said those laws had finally changed. "If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That's not true anymore. It's possible to make an equal marriage," she explained years later.Steinem also confessed to it being a "green card marriage" because Bale's US visa was running out - but said that they loved each other and were going to be together regardless.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, David Bale and Gloria Steinem, pictured with Maurine RothschildBale died three years later from brain lymphoma.Steinem had her own health scare with breast cancer in 1986, and underwent a lumpectomy.'So much to do'Gloria Steinem once said she wanted to live to 100 because "there's so much to do".In her near-century of life, she even became a talented tap dancer.She was given America's highest civilian honour - the Presidential Medal of Freedom - in 2013 by President Barack Obama, who credited her work with giving more women "the respect and opportunities that they deserve".In 2024, she reached the age of 90. She lived alone in New York, content in the knowledge that Ms. Magazine was still publishing.Steinem seized the occasion to tell the BBC that she hoped her legacy "might help individual people... to become more the unique, valuable, loved and lovable person that they want to be."She will be remembered for amplifying the voices of women in a way that mainstream media at the time either could not, or would not.And, in so doing, she altered the landscape and language of women's rights in America.

schema.headline: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism

title: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law
description: Nigel Farage's senior aide suggested a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of £500,000 for Reform UK, according to undercover
body: Nigel Farage's senior aide suggested a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of £500,000 for Reform UK, according to undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4.Dan Jukes was filmed meeting a man posing as the British-based son of a rich American businessman.Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.The undercover filming was done by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.Reform UK denies any wrongdoing and claims to have "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign funded climate change activists".The reporter posing as the son of the American donor is filmed raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.Filmed standing outside a pub in Westminster, Jukes said "you do realise that you can do it?"Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father. "Actually that does strike me as a solution," Jukes continues.He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before."That's one of the ways in which we do it," he is recorded as saying.Reform UK have launched an internal investigation into Jukes. They would not confirm if he remained a party spokesperson.Later, Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with both the reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor – his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Dan Jukes and the Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's Head of Policy, James Orr about it for some time."I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available.""Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.Orr is also now the subject of an internal Reform UK investigation.Earlier in Channel 4 News's film, prior to the suggested half a million pound donation, Channel 4 says Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps his father could pay for opinion polling to aide Reform's campaigning.The poll would cost £18,000 plus VAT – and Orr suggests that perhaps the polling company could send the bill to the undercover reporter.In all, Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.A Reform spokesperson said: "Reform UK has been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The party denies any wrongdoing."Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission."The hoaxers are 'Verbatim Investigations'; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Center for Climate Reporting (CCR). The methods of its founder, Lawrence Carter, have previously been rebuked by members of the United States Congress for videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation."An Electoral Commission spokesperson said: "The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500."Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider."A spokesman for the Metropolitan Police told the BBC: "We're aware of media reporting on Thursday, 3 September involving political party donations and an alleged breach of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 relating to polling. We will assess this matter and any information provided to us."It is understood the force has not begun an investigation.Jukes has been approached for comment.

schema.headline: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law

title: British army told to stop non-essential training exercises to save money
description: The Army has been told to stop "non-essential" training exercises to save money, according to a defence source.It will continue to train soldiers prep
body: The Army has been told to stop "non-essential" training exercises to save money, according to a defence source.It will continue to train soldiers preparing to be deployed or on deployments - such as units sent to Estonia, the Falklands or Cyprus.But units back in the UK and who are not preparing for a specific deployment have been told to cut back on collective training exercises due to financial pressures.It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to increase spending on defence.The government is increasing defence spending to 2.5% of national income by next year, but is under growing pressure to reach a target of 3% by the end of the decade.A defence source said the plans mean not doing what he called "nice to have training" - like large live fire exercises and rehearsing platoon attacks in UK training areas like Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire and Sennybridge in Wales. It is understood planned exercises that were due to take place that are now cancelled include one involving the Royal Tank Regiment conducting live fire drills in Wales and a separate exercise involving tanks and Apace helicopters.This was not the choice of the army, the source said. The pause is expected to continue for most of this year. Other specific training aimed at modernising the Army – such as practising drone and counter-drone warfare is expected to continue.The Army says it is prioritising the training that has been informed by lessons learnt from the war in Ukraine, and is reviewing each request for training on a case-by-case basis. Though the government is increasing defence spending, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) is still struggling to fund all its investment plans.Much of the new money has been earmarked for specific capital projects, including new weapons programmes. The part of the MoD's budget for training is still under significant pressure.An Army spokesperson said: "Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness."We are also investing £2bn to transform training for the British Army over the next 15 years."On Wednesday during Prime Minister's Questions, the chairman of the Commons Defence Select Committee, Labour's Tan Singh Dhesi, warned it was imperative to invest in the armed forces and urged Burnham to commit to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030. The prime minister replied: "I've made that commitment very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time."The government's wavering over defence spending was part of the downfall of Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer - with former Defence Secretary John Healey resigning his position in response to Sir Keir's plans on funding the armed forces. Plans set out in the Defence Investment Plan (Dip) will see defence spending rise to 2.7% of GDP by 2027/28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date.The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching both 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to "cut welfare spending and invest that money in our defence". The party says it would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030. "Faced with a choice between spending on military training and spending on benefits... Labour chooses more benefits," Tory shadow secretary of state for work and pensions Helen Whately said.

schema.headline: British army told to stop non-essential training exercises to save money

title: Reform UK promises £80bn of cuts to public spending
description: Reform UK has pledged to cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare, net zero policies, overseas aid and the number of civil s
body: Reform UK has pledged to cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare, net zero policies, overseas aid and the number of civil servants. Speaking from the party's conference in Birmingham, economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said he would like to cut taxes in Reform's first Budget if it wins power at the next election but would have to "earn the trust" of the markets first.Reform would be the "party of fiscal responsibility", he said and promised to make "big changes... in a careful way, not a cack-handed way". Labour said the proposed cuts were "incredibly reckless and could mean vital public services like hospitals, schools and law enforcement are put at risk".The bulk of Reform's proposed cuts come from its previously announced plans to reduce the welfare budget by £50bn. £10bn would be saved by cutting net zero programmes while £8bn would come from reducing the civil service and £7.1bn from capping the foreign aid budget.The party says its immigration policies, including abolishing indefinite leave to remain, would result in further savings.Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable. He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget"."Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and £45bn of tax cuts shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility.Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it. "It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.The triple lock is estimated to cost £15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector". He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere". Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high. Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy. Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a £5m gift he received before becoming an MP. There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party. The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

schema.headline: Reform UK promises £80bn of cuts to public spending

title: Zack Polanski says he'll run for former PM Starmer's seat in by-election
description: Green Party leader Zack Polanski has confirmed he wants to stand in the by-election brought about by Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP. Polanski
body: Green Party leader Zack Polanski has confirmed he wants to stand in the by-election brought about by Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP. Polanski, who is currently a London Assembly member but not a member of Parliament, said he was "so excited by the prospect" of being the first Green MP for Holborn and St Pancras. The Greens are targeting the seat, until now a Labour stronghold, after coming second to Labour in the area in local elections earlier this year.Sir Keir announced on Tuesday that he was quitting as MP for the London constituency, two months after he stood down as prime minister, setting up a challenging by-election for his successor Andy Burnham.In comments to the Camden New Journal, external on Thursday morning, Polanski said: "I have lived and worked in this community over many years, I know it well and I love it.""It's a clear fight between Labour and the Green Party," he added.Polanski has already been out campaigning in the constituency despite there being no decision on who the Green candidate will be until next week.In an interview with the BBC, he said: "We had a huge surge here in [local elections] in May. This is somewhere we can win."He said he wanted to be the Greens' sixth MP so he could "challenge Burnham constructively".In order to officially be the Green candidate for the seat, Polanski needs to be selected by local party members - something his comments suggest will happen.But there have been reports in recent days of splits among local Green activists, some of whom are said to favour a Palestinian candidate or a pro-Gaza independent.Andrew Feinstein, the independent runner-up to Sir Keir in the constituency at the 2024 general election, has appeared to back Polanski's candidacy as he ruled out running himself. Writing on X, Feinstein said: "Unfortunately I am not in a position to stand this time round."He said the Camden People's Alliance will meet next week to formally decide its position, adding: "This is a crucial time for progressives in Camden and across the country to be united."A date has not yet been set for the by-election.The stakes were already high for Labour at this by-election, because it offers an early test of Burnham's ability to stave off the Green threat in inner-city constituencies. With Polanski's candidacy, the stakes are even higher for the Greens, to see whether they make good on their leader's oft-stated ambition to replace Labour. Polanski said a Green victory would be a "clear message that we won't sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top".The London Assembly, on which Polanski currently sits, is an elected body of 25 representatives who scrutinise the policies of the mayor of London.

schema.headline: Zack Polanski says he'll run for former PM Starmer's seat in by-election

title: US billionaire Leon Black defies summons and sues Epstein panel
description: Billionaire investor Leon Black has failed to appear before a US congressional committee investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein - instead
body: Billionaire investor Leon Black has failed to appear before a US congressional committee investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein - instead filing a lawsuit challenging the committee's efforts to summon him.The lawsuit calls the subpoenas issued by the House Oversight Committee "invalid" and says they hold "no legitimate connection" to the committee's legislative aim.Black walked out of the committee in June while giving voluntary testimony after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time. Black has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein. The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June. His lawsuit opposing these summonses, which was filed in federal court in Washington on Thursday, argued that revealing the NDAs might "expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it". NDAs are contracts where both parties agree to keep information confidential, often as part of a settlement or employment agreement."This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr Black," Susan Estrich, an attorney for Black, said in a press release on Thursday."We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power." "By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two Congressional subpoenas," Robert Garcia, who sits on the committee, said in a statement after Black failed to appear. "His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable. We must hold him in contempt immediately," Garcia added.Contempt of Congress could result in the committee referring Black to the justice department for potential prosecution."It's a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people," Chairman Jomes Comer said. "Mr Black's testimony is crucial to our investigation."Black has said he employed Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling the House Oversight Committee in June that he had paid Epstein $158m (£120m) for legitimate purposes over the course of their years-long association.He has said he did not know about Epstein's "nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019". Black appears in the Epstein files released by the justice department, which include photos, videos and investigative documents relating to the disgraced late financier. There is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.Black had a six-year affair with a former Russian model, Guzel Ganieva, which ended in allegations of abuse, court records show.According to a lawsuit filed by Ganieva against Black, which was later dismissed, he prepared a nondisclosure agreement in 2015 to secure her silence.Epstein offered Black advice, including suggesting in an email to his assistant that Black hire former law enforcement officers to approach Ganieva, according to files released by the US justice department.Estrich, Black's attorney, has dismissed Ganieva's accusation as "demonstrably false". Black himself has previously said he was the victim of extortion.A judge ultimately dismissed Ganieva's lawsuit, citing the NDA she signed and about $9m (£6.6m) that she had received in the years after entering the agreement.Black left Apollo Global Management, a company he co-founded, in 2021 - saying at the time that "relentless public attention and media scrutiny" of his ties with Epstein had taken "a toll" on his health.

schema.headline: US billionaire Leon Black defies summons and sues Epstein panel

title: Kemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "kicking defence spending into the long grass" as she set out Tory plans to push t
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "kicking defence spending into the long grass" as she set out Tory plans to push the figure to 3% of GDP by 2030.Badenoch said a Conservative government would fund the commitment, worth £10bn a year, through measures including reimposing the two-child benefit cap, reforming housing benefit and ending VAT exemptions for Motability cars.Pointing to the threat from countries like Russia and Iran, Badenoch told a press conference: "Conflict is coming, we must act now."So far Andy Burnham's government has only committed to setting out a plan in the spring to meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.Speaking at an event in central London, Badenoch said: "Andy Burnham is kicking defence spending into the long grass."Our enemies are not going to sit around and wait for Labour to find the money to fight them."Burnham has pointed to his choice of Chancellor, John Healey, who quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, as proof of his commitment to defence investment.However, Badenoch said the prime minister should call a general election if he is not willing to find the money now, adding that Healey's decision to quit over defence spending appeared to have changed since he became chancellor."He resigned because Britain was not on track to reach 3% by 2030 and I praised him at the time for that decision," she said."Now that he is chancellor he does not seem to believe that any more and I am concerned he has been bought off with a promotion."Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap. The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April, meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.The Tories said this would include saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving £1bn."Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with £37.3bn forecast to be spent. The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this."It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC."Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era."Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe. "In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030."Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.

schema.headline: Kemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass

title: Falkland Islands: Donald Trump hints US would not back UK over Argentina
description: Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.In an interview with
body: Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.In an interview with GB News, the US president said that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran, despite later saying his military did not need any support.Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.Argentinian President Javier Milei is due to make a televised statement on Thursday night about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory. When asked if he would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump told GB News: "Well look, I was there when they had the first war."That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away."Turning his attention to the US' current conflict with Iran, he added: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me."Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'Trump said the-then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad", he added.He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get – most of those countries get – a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves". Argentina and the UK waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.Seventy-four days of fighting led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.Trump's comments come after he was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the islands.The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

schema.headline: Falkland Islands: Donald Trump hints US would not back UK over Argentina

title: Three farmers detained by Israel in Lebanon, village leader says
description: Three Lebanese farmers have been detained by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon, according to the leader of their village.Issa Abedelaal told the BBC
body: Three Lebanese farmers have been detained by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon, according to the leader of their village.Issa Abedelaal told the BBC that Israeli forces called the three farmers on their mobile phones and instructed them to report to a location, where they were detained and taken away.It came after Israeli forces had entered the village of Halta in Hasbaya province, which lies within a roughly 600 sq km area that Israel continues to occupy.The detentions were reported to the US-led International Monitoring and Implementation Mechanism, which oversees security coordination between Israel and Lebanon. The Israeli military has not replied to a request for comment.Hours later, Israel released another Lebanese civilian held in the country, in what is believed to be the first known civilian release since US-mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon began in April.Malek Ghazi was handed over to the Lebanese army by the International Committee of the Red Cross, while Israel says four more Lebanese civilians will be released on Friday.More than 30 Lebanese are still believed to be in Israeli custody, as negotiations between the two countries remain stalled over a framework involving Hezbollah's disarmament, an Israeli withdrawal and the deployment of the Lebanese army in the south.Ghazi was handed over at the Naqoura crossing before being taken to an army intelligence facility in Tyre for a medical examination.His family says he disappeared last October after leaving home to exercise.Israel's prime minister's office said four other civilians due to be released on Friday had been questioned and found to have no links to armed groups.Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam welcomed Ghazi's release and thanked the US for its role in securing it.He said the government would continue working for the release of all Lebanese detainees, information about those still missing, and a complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory.The detainee issue is part of wider US-mediated negotiations, alongside separate efforts to recover the remains of Lebanese Jewish community leaders abducted and killed during the country's civil war.The negotiations also cover a framework agreed in mid-June, under which Hezbollah is expected to disarm, the Lebanese army to deploy in the south and Israeli forces to withdraw gradually, beginning with designated "pilot zones".But the process has made little headway, with Israel questioning the role of the Lebanese army and disagreements over how compliance would be verified.Hezbollah rejects the talks and the pilot-zone concept outright.The two sides have yet to set a date for the eighth round of talks.Israel has continued attacks on southern Lebanon, and officials say the Israeli military has been expanding its positions.Lebanese authorities said 11 people were killed in an Israeli air strike on the region in August. Israel's Defense Forces (IDF) said at the time that it had killed a Hezbollah commander in the strike, following an attack against Israeli soldiers.

schema.headline: Three farmers detained by Israel in Lebanon, village leader says

title: How a fly brain may help explain the secrets of human behaviour
description: Scientists have managed to compare the fine detail of the brains of male and female flies for the first time, identifying differences they say explain
body: Scientists have managed to compare the fine detail of the brains of male and female flies for the first time, identifying differences they say explain male aggression, courtship and their singing of love songs.The scientists in Cambridge mapped all 124 million connections of nerve cells in a male fly's brain, having done the same for a female fly two years ago.The team are clear that the research won't explain differences between men and women because our behaviour is far more complex.But the research could help scientists better understand human behaviour and conditions in which genetic differences affect brain wiring, such as autism and schizophrenia.Prof Gregory Jefferis, of the Medical Research Council's Laboratory of Molecular Biology and University of Cambridge, who co-led the research, told BBC News that the breakthrough was "a really important new avenue in neuroscience", likening it to the invention of a powerful new telescope in increasing our understanding of the Universe."We have this amazing stuff in our heads that lets us do incredible things such as playing a sonata or solving a scientific problem. And this development could help our understanding of how those  systems work".The small differences they discovered can lead to big changes in behaviour.In courtship, for example, the male tracks the female as she moves. The researchers have identified the brain circuits associated with that trait and found key differences in the wiring. The males have extra bits that should enhance his visual tracking.There is an even bigger difference in the circuits associated with aggression. Males fight more often and so there is much more wiring associated with that behaviour than in females.And then, there is the love song circuit.Males woo females by producing a sound. They have wiring unique only to them to producee the sound. According to Dr Philipp Schlegel, co-author of the study, the circuit has to be just right, otherwise the consequneces for the poor male could be dire."The courtship also includes singing to the female," he told me. "The sound is produced by vibrating the wings to produce a very specific song."If the female likes it, she will allow him to approach, and if she doesn't, and she's not receptive at a time, she'll basically reject him, which could be a kick to the face".These three differences between male and female wiring in flies are driven by two key genes. Researchers have known about the genes for years, and how they're linked to each of these behaviours. What they've never been able to see is the bit in the middle. Now, for the first time, they can see the actual wiring those genes produce.The primary aim of the research was not to discover the differences between male and female flies, and certainly not to find neurological explanations for certain alleged behavioural differences between men and women. Comparing two brains that have some slight wiring differences associated with known big behavioural differences enables scientists to clearly see the principles that underlie the changes to brain wiring for all behaviour, according to Beckett."You just have one independent variable, the sex, and then you can see what's different. This is a scientist's dream".These differences take scientists a big step forward in understanding one of the biggest questions in biology - how genes influence behaviour. Scientists have known for decades that they do, but have had little idea of exactly how they exert their influence. The answer, according to Dr Jefferis, is in how the genes shape the brain's wiring and how that wiring influences behaviour."The fly brain comparison gives us a really good handle on this," he told BBC News."There are patterns of behaviour in humans that seem to have a strong genetic, basis. So, for example, there are many gene varients now related to schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders that we don't really understand".

schema.headline: How a fly brain may help explain the secrets of human behaviour

title: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills
description: Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas s
body: Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas stores before the weather dips.Wholesale natural gas prices are already at three-year highs, which could lead to increased energy bills for businesses and consumers.Europe, which delayed its summer stockpiling due to high wholesale costs sparked by the Iran war, had been gambling the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall. Storage levels are significantly lower than usual for this time of year, with countries facing the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.The European benchmark natural gas price topped €75/MWh on Wednesday, its highest level since late 2022, the tail end of a spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Natural gas prices in the UK this week topped 185p per therm, also the highest since late 2022.The price has jumped in the past week amid a return to hostilities between the US and Iran, with analysts fearing the renewed fighting will keep the key Strait of Hormuz closed even longer. Typically, around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is transported through the waterway.Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said he did not expect the waterway to begin reopening until early 2027.Even then, there will be a lag before energy is flowing freely through the strait and pressure on energy prices are eased. "The risks to gas prices are definitely tilted towards the upside," Hussain told the BBC, warning that the gas price would top €80 by the end of this year.Hussain recalled interviews with gas storage operators at the outbreak of the US-Israeli war in Iran saying they would wait three to four months for the crisis to ease before stocking up. "We are about six months into the strait being effectively closed and that obviously has not happened," he added.Higher wholesale gas prices feed through to household energy bills by helping determine regulator Ofgem's price cap.The energy price cap rose in July, and will increase by 4% in October, leaving a typical household paying £1,723. But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices could rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, told the BBC on Thursday  a fresh increase in wholesale prices would "increase pressure on our January price cap forecast". However, he cautioned that there was "plenty of time to go" and a fall in wholesale prices could ease the pressure.The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) said gas prices are determined on international markets, dismissing criticism of the UK's own low levels of storage.The boss of British Gas owner Centrica, Chris O'Shea, has repeatedly called for support from the government to expand its Rough storage facility in the North Sea, warning it has been unviable to fill it up and that it will close next year without a deal."We have almost no gas in storage in the UK for the coming winter and this is a huge concern as energy security is national security," he said on LinkedIn, external last week.A DESNZ spokesman said: "We remain open to discussing proposals on all gas storage sites, as long as it provides value for money for taxpayers."The department also pointed to Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge to cut VAT from energy bills from October, as well as government action to reduce Britain's reliance on natural gas altogether.Ángel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, said there is a "glass half full, and a glass half empty" picture unfolding. On one hand, wholesale gas prices are significantly lower than during the crisis which followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.On the other, households and businesses will still face significantly higher energy bills than usual over the coming months. "It's serious, but not catastrophic," he told the BBC, adding "something would have to dramatically change to lower prices".He pointed to a reduction in demand for natural gas in general as a result of the shift towards renewables, but said the overall picture depends hugely on the winter weather."If you have a warmer winter than average, that will be great for demand," he said. But he warned a colder than average winter would have the opposite effect, driving up demand for energy and pushing up prices.It is not known how the developing El Niño over the Pacific Ocean will impact Britain's winter. The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009-10 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.However, 2006-07 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.Talavera said gas prices could come down if the weather helps reduce demand and the Strait of Hormuz reopens sooner than expected. But, at the moment, "the weather machine remains our main hope". It comes as a recent spike in the UK government's borrowing costs eased. After a sharp uptick on Tuesday, which took the yield on a 10-year bond - or gilt - to the highest level since 2008, it fell back slightly on Thursday. Yields are hovering around 5.15%, however, which would still represent a post-2008 peak were it not for Tuesday's jump.

schema.headline: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills

title: US Open 2026 results: Harriet Dart struggles with illness in Marie Bouzkova loss
description: Britain's Harriet Dart said she felt "under the weather" as she struggled in the heat during her second-round loss to Marie Bouzkova at the US Open.Da
body: Britain's Harriet Dart said she felt "under the weather" as she struggled in the heat during her second-round loss to Marie Bouzkova at the US Open.Dart struggled for rhythm in a 6-2 6-2 defeat by Czech 25th seed Bouzkova as temperatures reached around 30C in New York. Dart's defeat means Fran Jones is the last remaining Briton in either singles draw at Flushing Meadows.Jones faces American 14th seed Iva Jovic later on Thursday.Dart draped ice towels around her neck and used cold-air hoses at the changeovers against Bouzkova as she attempted to cool down."I have been a bit under the weather. It is what it is, sadly," Dart, 30, said."It was quite warm. I had a temperature, I was trying to cool down. I've played many weeks in a row. "I am not used to air conditioning being pumped everywhere. We go from really hot outside to freezing inside."All credit to my opponent, she is an incredibly tough player, so even if I had been at full capacity, I don't know."Dart, who is ranked 131st in the world, struggled on serve against Bouzkova, committing eight double faults and landing only 45% of her first serves.Bouzkova took command almost straight away, winning seven games in a row to clinch the first set and go a double break up in the second.From there Dart was unable to recover as Bouzkova safely saw out the rest of the match to reach the third round, where she will face Polish eighth seed Iga Swiatek. Dart's exit follows compatriot Katie Boulter's second-round defeat by Karolina Muchova in only 58 minutes on Wednesday.In the men's draw, Jacob Fearnley and Toby Samuel lost in the second round, while Cameron Norrie, Arthur Fery, Harry Wendelken and Jan Choinski exited in the first round.

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Harriet Dart struggles with illness in Marie Bouzkova loss

title: Jive Bunny And The Mastermixers creator John Pickles dies at 84
description: Jive Bunny And The Mastermixers were made up of Pickles, his son Andrew, who also worked as a director for Mastermix, along with Doncaster DJ and prod
body: Jive Bunny And The Mastermixers were made up of Pickles, his son Andrew, who also worked as a director for Mastermix, along with Doncaster DJ and producer Les Hemstock.The group also had a UK top 10 album in Jive Bunny The Album and scored five UK top 10 hits, including their number ones.The Jive Bunny album covers and music videos featured a cartoon rabbit, with costumed actors also making promotional appearances as the character.Steve White, a DJ who knew Pickles personally, told BBC Radio Sheffield the group's chart success had been "a people's success story"."It was something that the family could enjoy," White said.In December 2024, Mastermix released a new Jive Bunny production called 3, 6, 9.It was said by the company to be "celebrating the origins of Jive Bunny while adding a modern twist".

schema.headline: Jive Bunny And The Mastermixers creator John Pickles dies at 84

title: Richarlison: Tottenham omit Brazil forward from Premier League squad
description: Richarlison has been left out of Tottenham's Premier League squad.Spurs manager Roberto de Zerbi said last week the Brazil forward had asked to leave
body: Richarlison has been left out of Tottenham's Premier League squad.Spurs manager Roberto de Zerbi said last week the Brazil forward had asked to leave the club and he looked close to joining former club Everton before Tuesday's transfer deadline, but a deal fell through.The 29-year-old has now been left out the club's squad to play in top-flight games for the first half of the season.It is understood Richarlison does not feature in Tottenham's plans this season, which was explained to the player before Tuesday's deadline.He is expected to leave the club in the coming days, with the transfer windows in Turkey and Saudi Arabia still open.Richarlison joined Tottenham from Everton in the summer of 2022, having joined the Toffees from Watford in 2018.He has entered the final year of his contract at the London club and, while he started Tottenham's defeat by Brentford in their opening game of the Premier League season, he was not included in De Zerbi's squad when Spurs lost 2-0 at home to Newcastle United on Saturday.After the game, De Zerbi said: "Richarlison, I don't know. He said too many times he wants to leave."Earlier in August, the Spurs boss said that the Brazilian was uncertain about his future, noting that "it's not easy to find another striker like Richarlison".However, Spurs recently signed Manchester City striker Omar Marmoush on loan and he replaced Richarlison against Newcastle.Richarlison was Tottenham's top scorer in the league last season with 11 goals in 32 appearances and also provided four assists as he was a key figure during their struggle for Premier League survival, which was secured on the final day.

schema.headline: Richarlison: Tottenham omit Brazil forward from Premier League squad

title: Fifa accuses Uefa of 'smear campaign' against Gianni Infantino
description: Fifa has accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to litigation over president Gianni Infantino's scrapped plan
body: Fifa has accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to litigation over president Gianni Infantino's scrapped plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.Last week European football's governing body filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa as part of potential criminal claims in Switzerland.In a dramatic escalation of the controversy, Uefa accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" and "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by [him] for his own benefit" over the now-shelved Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme.However, world governing body Fifa has now responded with court filings lodged in the US - and seen by the BBC - requesting that permission for access to documents be deferred, or opposed by the end of the month. Fifa claims Uefa's argument "suffers from a fundamental defect" and "legal deficiencies". "Uefa seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that Uefa admittedly lacks the authority to initiate. Despite that threshold problem, Uefa asks this court to authorise sweeping discovery about the FFE."It said it had "made clear" that the creation of FFE was "only a proposal", adding that it could have only proceeded on the condition that the majority of member associations supported it and "the relevant approvals of the Fifa Council"."Rather than participate in that democratic process, Uefa issued a press release - the beginning of a weeks-long smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership," it wrote in the court filing.It also claimed that Uefa's "economic motivation" was to prevent smaller countries from having the "financial strength to compete with the European elite"."If soccer is strengthened in the developing world, global competition increases, which ultimately reduces Uefa's market power and provides more competition for its flagship tournaments," Fifa said."By raising funds to allow some of Fifa's smaller member associations to better develop soccer, FFE would lead to more players from those nations choosing to represent their countries of origin and playing in their home leagues rather than playing abroad."Uefa has declined to comment, although BBC Sport has been told insiders believe that if Fifa has nothing to hide, it should disclose the documents and speed up the legal process. It has led the rebellion against the Fifa president, who is facing calls to stand down from three confederations.Uefa has also asked a court in New York to approve a legal document ordering testimony and documents from venture capitalist Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, who was set to be the lead investor in FFE, and his company Thrive Eternal.Thrive had held talks with Infantino about heading up a $4.2bn (£3.1bn) investment in 20% of a new Fifa commercial subsidiary, before the idea was abandoned days after it was revealed in July amid a huge backlash.At the time, Fifa claimed FFE would have increased the funding distributed to each national association for the 2027-2030 cycle from £5.9m to £14.7m.On Sunday, Kushner expressed regret over FFE, saying: "While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to… had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved."Uefa has also asked for the disclosure of documents from American financier Greg Maffei, who was a key adviser on the deal. While Uefa says neither Kushner nor Maffei are anticipated defendants in any legal proceedings, it claims the pair first discussed the FFE concept in July 2025 and that Infantino had "been discussing the underlying concept with Kushner for nearly a year before the terms sheet was ultimately signed".Its lawyers also argue the World Cup was deliberately undervalued at about £15bn, which it says is "a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer". Uefa claims Infantino failed to consult Fifa's hierarchy over the plan.

schema.headline: Fifa accuses Uefa of 'smear campaign' against Gianni Infantino
